newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Panjsher Valley readies for war.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Panjsher Valley readies for war.

text.p: Ethnic Tajik fighters loyal to famed guerrilla chief Ahmad Shah Masood worked furiously on Tuesday to prepare the defence of their Panjsher Valley against an expected assault by Afghanistan's hardline Islamist Taleban militia.

Bundled out of Kabul on Friday by an unexpectedly swift advance by the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban and attacked by former allies during their retreat, Masood's men appeared demoralised but ready to defend their homeland.
Throughout the 1980s, they repulsed repeated Soviet attempts to capture the long valley, where broad green patches surrounding villages are interspersed with narrow, rocky defiles.

Masood's aides at his headquarters in the valley, whose location they asked not to be disclosed, said they were talking to northern Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum about an alliance against the Taleban. They declined to say how far the talks had gone or provide any further details.
They said their retreat from Kabul had been rapid because former allies had turned against Masood, military chief of the ousted government, and they had been forced to fight their way north.
Masood's men had been prepared to make a stand at Charikar, some 60 kms (40 miles) north of Kabul, but had been attacked from behind before the Taleban forces arrived, the aides said.

Masood's forces had abandoned a major base and large amounts of equipment just north of the town, then retreated to Jabal as-Seraj about 10 km (six miles) to the north near the narrow entrance to the Panjsher valley but had been too disorganised to mount a stand, they said.

So they had abandoned more military equipment and taken what they could inside the valley before planting dynamite to bring a landslide down across the road in the gorge that leads into the valley, they added.

Inside the valley on Tuesday, hundreds of people mere packing what they could carry and climbing over the rock-strewn road impassable to vehicles to get away from what they feared would be a major Taleban offensive.

Taleban acting Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammed Stanakzai told reporters in Kabul on Tuesday that the militia had decided to attack the valley because Masood's presence there with large quantities of arms and ammunition was "strategically dangerous".

Taleban commander Abdur Razzaq told Reuters in Jabal os-Siraj that the assault would be launched unless Masood surrendered, but there were no signs amoung the Tajiks that they were prepared to do that.

Masood's men were busy blowing up sections of the road and reinforcing strong positions on the valley floor and on the steep, treeless mountainsides unused since the Soviet army quit Afghanistan in 1989.

It is easy to see why the Soviet army had such a tough time in the Panjsher valley, with its twists and turns and sudden narrowings and there was no suggestion that the Taleban would have it any easier.
Masood's aides said he had stocked plenty of ammunition and fuel in the vally and had flown helicopters there as the ousted government pulled out of Kabul, although they would not say how many.
They said Masood also had some Soviet-era fighter planes at Kunduz, just north of Panjsher, but again would not say how many.
